## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a20-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- a20-ideas:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Two kinds of question</dt><dd>Exploratory scenarios ask what happens if their assumptions hold; a target-seeking one asks what it would take to meet a goal.</dd><dt>The spread is information</dt><dd>Prairieland's four end 2050 between 65.9 Mt and 290.1 Mt of CO₂; none of them is a forecast.</dd><dt>Gaps have causes</dt><dd>From Announced plans to Gas boom, the four groups alone add up to +170.3 Mt against a real gap of +123.2 Mt.</dd><dt>Order matters</dt><dd>Swapping technology costs adds 0.0 Mt to +56.3 Mt, depending on the order; its average over the 24 orders is +23.2 Mt.</dd><dt>The policy is an output</dt><dd>The Budget pathway's 2,600 Mt budget is fixed; its carbon price, $84 a tonne, is found.</dd></dl>
<!-- a20-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The accounting behind the four scenarios</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Demand.** Each sector's [useful energy]{.lx-term term="useful-energy"} grows at its demand case's rate; a share of it switches to electricity at the policy's pace, up to Prairieland's limits.
- **Existing plants** run as in 2025 until their retirement year; from 2030, a coal or combined-cycle plant closes early when its fuel and carbon cost per MWh is above the clean mix's full cost.
- **New power.** The rest is shared between new gas plants and a clean mix (wind, solar, the generic firm clean plant, batteries) by their full costs per MWh:

$$s = \min\left(1,\ \max\left(0,\ \tfrac{1}{2} + \frac{C_{\text{gas}} - C_{\text{clean}}}{2W}\right)\right), \qquad C = \frac{K \cdot \mathrm{CRF}(r, n) + F}{\mathit{cf} \times 8.76} + V$$

- **Symbols**, in the table below; $C$ is a plant's full cost per MWh.

::: {.a20-sym}
| Symbol | What it is | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $s$ | the clean share of new power | 0 to 1 |
| $W$ | the rule's half-width: the cost gap at which all or none of new power is clean | \$ per MWh |
| $K$ | capital cost | \$ per kW |
| $F$ | fixed upkeep | \$ per kW a year |
| $V$ | variable cost; for gas, also fuel and the carbon price | \$ per MWh |
| $\mathit{cf}$ | [capacity factor]{.lx-term term="capacity-factor"} | 0 to 1 |
| $\mathrm{CRF}(r, n)$ | the [capital recovery factor]{.lx-term term="capital-recovery-factor"}, $r / (1 - (1 + r)^{-n})$: the share of $K$ paid each year | per year |
| $r$, $n$ | the discount rate; the life | per year; years |
| 8.76 | the MWh one kW makes in a year at full output (8,760 hours ÷ 1,000) | MWh per kW |
:::
- **Fixed costs.** Every capital cost is a fixed value inside Prairieland's range, the same in 2030 and 2050; none changes with how much is built.
- **Imports and CO₂.** Domestic oil and gas output stay at 2025's levels, so extra fuel is imported; CO₂ uses the IPCC's default factors for fuel burned.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Splitting a gap fairly when causes interact</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **One at a time.** Each change alone, from the same start: simple, but the parts need not add up to the gap.
- **In order.** Each change after the ones before it: the parts add up exactly, but they depend on the order.
- **The average over every order.** Four groups have 24 orders; each group's step averaged over all of them gives shares that add up to the gap (the Shapley value of game theory).
- **Index decomposition.** For identities such as CO₂ = population × income × energy intensity × carbon intensity, the logarithmic mean Divisia index splits a change with no residual (Ang 2015, [Energy Policy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enpol.2015.07.007)).
- **Report the method.** Whichever you use, say so beside the bars.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Where a national budget comes from</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **A target is chosen.** A target-seeking scenario needs a target first; a national carbon budget is one, and choosing it is a value judgement, not a model output.
- **Sharing a global budget.** Common rules give each country a share by population, by today's emissions, by capability to pay or by historical responsibility; each rule gives a very different national budget.
- **Prairieland's reference budgets.** Step 7 lists three, arithmetic on 2025's emissions (no change, or a straight line to zero by 2050 or 2040), not a fair share under any rule.
- **Report the rule.** A study that cites a national budget should say which sharing rule, which global budget and which start year it used.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>How an optimization model seeks a target</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **A budget is a rule.** A planning model adds one constraint: the sum over the model years of weight × emissions stays at or below the budget.
- **Its price.** In a least-cost model the constraint's [shadow price]{.lx-term term="shadow-price"} is what one more tonne of budget would save; the model finds plan and price together.
- **This page's price.** Its [implied carbon price]{.lx-term term="implied-carbon-price"} is the lowest whole-dollar price that meets the budget under the sharing rule, found by trying prices; it need not equal a model's shadow price.
- **Foresight.** A model that sees every period at once plans differently from one that plans decade by decade; that choice is one more assumption to report.
- **Next.** Modeler lesson [M13](m13-national-pathway.html) builds Prairieland's multi-region, multi-decade model; the [Pathway Explorer (SB4)](sb4-pathway-explorer.html) lets you run it.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Hourly balance, storage timing, transmission between regions and adequacy: the job of a planning model such as <a href="m13-national-pathway.html">M13</a>'s.</li>
<li>How prices respond to demand, and how people and firms respond to prices beyond the sharing rule.</li>
<li>The cost of heat pumps, vehicles and other end-use equipment.</li>
<li>Methane and other gases, land use and carbon removal.</li>
<li>Probabilities: this lesson assigns none, so its results do not tell us which scenario is more likely.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 30 minutes: four myths, then six exercises with worked answers.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a20-myth">
<!-- a20-myths:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="forecast" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An energy outlook is a forecast of what will happen.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. EIA says the results of its Annual Energy Outlook 2026 are not predictions; the IEA calls its scenarios exploratory or normative.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wrong" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “When two outlooks disagree, at least one of them is wrong.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Both can be consistent: Current policies and the Budget pathway answer different questions with the same data.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="target" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A target-seeking scenario shows what will happen once a country adopts the target.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It shows one way to meet the target under its assumptions: with Gas boom's cheap gas, the Budget pathway needs $134 a tonne instead of $84 a tonne.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="split" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A gap between two scenarios splits into parts that do not depend on how you split it.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. When assumptions interact, the parts depend on the order: here, swapping technology costs adds 0.0 Mt to +56.3 Mt.</p></details>
</div>
<!-- a20-myths:end -->
</div>
```

```{=html}
<tr><td class="n">2 + 2</td><td>The IEA's World Energy Outlook 2025 has two exploratory scenarios (Current Policies, Stated Policies) and two normative ones (Net Zero Emissions by 2050, ACCESS).</td><td class="s"><a href="https://www.iea.org/commentaries/scenarios-in-the-world-energy-outlook-2025">IEA commentary</a> · read 2 Nov 2026</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">Dec 2025</td><td>The laws and regulations in force that EIA's Annual Energy Outlook 2026 Counterfactual Baseline case assumes; EIA says its results are not predictions.</td><td class="s"><a href="https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/aeo/narrative/index.php">EIA, AEO2026 narrative</a> · 8 Apr 2026</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">1990–2014</td><td>The years of the UK's electricity transition that Trutnevyte (2016) compared with cost-optimal scenarios: the least-cost answer departed from what happened.</td><td class="s"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2016.03.038">Energy 106</a> · 2016</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>The IEA's World Energy Outlook 2025 (November 2025) reports exploratory and normative scenarios side by side, and EIA's Annual Energy Outlook 2026 (8 April 2026) adds side cases on growth, oil and gas supply and technology costs.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Comparing one outlook's exploratory scenario with another's normative one compares answers to different questions. This lesson makes no claim about which outlook is right.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>International Energy Agency. <a href="https://www.iea.org/commentaries/scenarios-in-the-world-energy-outlook-2025">Scenarios in the World Energy Outlook 2025</a> (commentary): which scenarios are exploratory and which normative (read 2 November 2026).</li>
<li>U.S. Energy Information Administration. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/aeo/narrative/index.php">Annual Energy Outlook 2026, narrative</a>: foreword and introduction, the Counterfactual Baseline case and the side cases. Released 8 April 2026.</li>
<li>U.S. Energy Information Administration. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/aeo/assumptions/pdf/EMM_Assumptions.pdf">Assumptions to the Annual Energy Outlook 2026: Electricity Market Module</a>, Tables 3 and 4: the capital costs behind Prairieland's ranges (2025 dollars).</li>
<li>IPCC (2006). <a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/2006-ipcc-guidelines-for-national-greenhouse-gas-inventories/">2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories</a>, Volume 2, Energy: default CO₂ factors.</li>
<li>Trutnevyte, E. (2016). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2016.03.038">Does cost optimization approximate the real-world energy transition?</a> Energy 106, 182–193.</li>
<li>DeCarolis, J. F., et al. (2017). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2017.03.001">Formalizing best practice for energy system optimization modelling</a>. Applied Energy 194, 184–198.</li>
<li>Ang, B. W. (2015). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enpol.2015.07.007">LMDI decomposition approach: A guide for implementation</a>. Energy Policy 86, 233–238.</li>
<li>Prairieland: the course's shared national data (prairieland.json), with the sources listed there. The four scenarios and the sharing rule: set for teaching.</li>
</ul>
</div>
```
